exampleAnswers.title: Limits at Infinity of Reciprocal Functions

question.text: If the figure above shows the graph of $g(x),$ then
question.explanation:
Applying the product rule, we have \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty}\dfrac{g(x)}{x^{2}} &=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty} \left(g(x) \cdot \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)\\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty} g(x) \cdot \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}. \end{align*}

From the graph, we get that $\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty} g(x)=-2.$ Therefore, the above becomes: \[ \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty}\dfrac{g(x)}{x^{2}}= -2 \cdot \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^{2}} \]

Now, using the fact that \[ \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right)=0, \] we can evaluate our limit as follows: \[ -2\cdot\lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2} = -2\cdot 0 = 0 \]

Therefore, we conclude that \[ \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty}\dfrac{g(x)}{x^{2}}=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{0}. \]

example.title: Limits at Infinity of Reciprocal Functions

question.explanation:
First, we use the algebra of limits to pull out the constant factor of $-7 \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \left(-\dfrac{7}{x^5}\right) &= \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \left(-7 \cdot \dfrac{1}{x^5}\right)\\[5pt] &= -7 \cdot\lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^5} \end{align*}

Now, using the fact that

\[ \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^5} = 0, \]

we can evaluate our limit as follows:

\[ -7 \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^5} = -7 \cdot 0 = 0 \]

question.explanation:
First, we use the algebra of limits to pull out the constant factor of $-3\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \dfrac{-3}{x^8} &= \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left[ -3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{x^8} \right] \\[5pt] &= -3 \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{x^8} \end{align*}

Now, using the fact that

\[ \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left( \dfrac{1}{x^8} \right) = 0, \]

we can evaluate our limit as follows:

\[ -3 \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{x^8} = -3 \cdot 0 = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{0} \]

exampleAnswers.title: Limits at Infinity of Reciprocals of Polynomials

question.explanation:
First, we rewrite our limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

\[ \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow -\infty} \dfrac{-4}{(x^2 - 3)^3} = -4 \cdot \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow -\infty} \dfrac{1}{(x^2 - 3)^3} \]

For any non-constant polynomial $P(x),$ we have

\[ \lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{P(x)}\right) = 0. \]

Therefore, since $(x^2 - 3)^3$ is a non-constant polynomial, we have \[ \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{(x^2 - 3)^3} = 0. \]

Finally, we can evaluate the original limit as follows:

\[ -4 \cdot \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow -\infty} \dfrac{1}{(x^2 - 3)^3} = -4 \cdot 0 = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{0} \]

question.text: If the figure above shows the graph of $g(x),$ then
question.explanation:
From the diagram, $\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty} g(x)=-2.$

Now, rewrite the target limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty}\dfrac{g(x)}{x^{3}-2x^2-7} &= \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty} g(x)\cdot \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow -\infty}\dfrac{1}{x^{3}-2x^2-7} \end{align*}

For any non-constant polynomial $P(x),$ we have \[ \lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{P(x)}\right) = 0. \]

Therefore, since $x^{3}$ is a non-constant polynomial, we have \[ \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{x^{3}-2x^2-7} = 0. \]

Finally, we can evaluate the original limit as follows: \begin{align} \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} g(x) \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{x^{3}-2x^2-7} = -2 \cdot 0 = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{0} \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Infinite Limits of Reciprocal Functions Where the Leading Term Has an Odd Power

question.explanation:
First, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows: \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0^-} \left(\dfrac{7}{9x^7}\right)} &= \dfrac{7}{9}\cdot \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0^-} \dfrac{1}{x^7}} \end{align*}

Now, recall the fact that \[ \lim_\limits{x \to 0^-} \dfrac{1}{x^7} = -\infty. \]

The positive factor of $\dfrac{7}{9}$ does not change the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that \[ \dfrac{7}{9}\cdot \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0^-} \dfrac{1}{x^7}} = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{-\infty}. \]

example.title: Infinite Limits of Reciprocal Functions Where the Leading Term Has an Odd Power

question.explanation:
First, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{7}{3x}}&=\dfrac{7}{3}\cdot \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{1}{x}} \end{align*}

Now, recall the fact that

\[ \lim_\limits{x \to 0^-} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)=-\infty, \qquad \lim_\limits{x \to 0^+} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)=\infty. \]

We conclude that \[ \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)}=\text{DNE}. \]

Therefore, \[ \dfrac{7}{3}\cdot \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{1}{x}} = \text{DNE}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Infinite Limits of Reciprocal Functions Where the Leading Term Has an Even Power

question.explanation:
First, we simplify the limit:

\[ \lim_\limits{x \to 0^+} \dfrac9 {12x^4} = \lim_\limits{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{3}{4x^4} \]

Then, we use the algebra of limits to pull out the constant factor of $\dfrac 34\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{3}{4x^4} &= \lim_\limits{x \to 0^+} \dfrac 3 4 \cdot\dfrac{1}{x^4}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 3 4 \cdot\lim_\limits{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{1}{x^4}\\[5pt] \end{align*}

We recall the graph of the function $y=\dfrac 1 {x^4}$

From the graph, we see that

\[ \lim_\limits{x \to (0^+)} \dfrac{1}{x^4} = \infty \]

The positive factor of $\dfrac 3 4$ does not change the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that

\[ \dfrac{3}{4} \cdot\lim_\limits{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{1}{x^4} =\infty. \]

example.title: Infinite Limits of Reciprocal Functions Where the Leading Term Has an Even Power

question.explanation:
First, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows: \[ \displaystyle{\lim_{x \to 5^-} \left(-\dfrac{9}{4(x-5)^6}\right)} \;=\; -\dfrac{9}{4}\,\cdot\, \lim_{x \to 5^-} \dfrac{1}{(x-5)^6}. \]

Now, we can sketch the graph of $y = \dfrac{1}{(x-5)^6}$ as follows:

  1. Take the graph of $y = \dfrac 1 {x^6}.$

  2. Translate it to the right by $5$ units. This gives $y =\dfrac{1}{(x-5)^6},$ as shown below.

From the graph, we see that \[ \lim_\limits{x \to 5^-} \dfrac{1}{(x-5)^6} = \infty. \]

Finally, the negative factor of $-\dfrac{9}{4}$ changes the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that \[ -\dfrac{9}{4} \cdot \lim_{x \to 5^-} \dfrac{1}{(x-5)^6} = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{-\infty}. \]

Now, we recall the graph of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{x^8} \mathbin{:}$

From the graph, we see that \[ \lim_\limits{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{1}{x^8} = \infty. \]

Finally, the negative factor of $-\dfrac{9}{5}$ changes the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that \[ -\dfrac{9}{5} \cdot \lim_{x \to 0^+} \dfrac{1}{x^8} = -\infty. \]

example.title: Infinite Limits of Reciprocal Functions Where the Leading Term Has an Even Power

question.explanation:
We can sketch the graph of $y = \dfrac{1}{(x-1)^2}$ as follows:

  1. Take the graph of $y = \dfrac 1 {x^2}.$

  2. Translate it to the right by $1$ unit. This gives $y = \dfrac{1}{(x-1)^2},$ as shown below.

From the graph, we see that

\[ \lim_\limits{x \to (1^-)} \dfrac{1}{(x-1)^2} = \infty, \qquad \lim_\limits{x \to (1^+)} \dfrac{1}{(x-1)^2} = \infty, \]

and therefore

\[ \lim_\limits{x \to 1} \dfrac{1}{(x-1)^2}= \infty. \]
